item.title: Six Core Principles of AI-Native Infrastructure
item.description:
Introduction

The term “AI-native infrastructure” has become increasingly common, but what does it actually mean to build infrastructure that is native to AI workloads? Having spent years working on cloud-native systems and now deeply embedded in AI infrastructure, I’ve identified six core principles that define truly AI-native infrastructure.

1. Substrate-Compatible

AI-native infrastructure doesn’t replace cloud-native systems — it extends them. Kubernetes remains the substrate. Container runtimes, service meshes, and observability stacks all continue to play their roles. What changes is the semantic layer on top.

item.title: GPU Virtualization in Kubernetes with HAMi
item.description:
The GPU Utilization Problem

In most Kubernetes clusters running AI workloads, GPU utilization is surprisingly low. A common pattern: a team requests a full GPU for their inference service, but actual utilization hovers around 15-30%. The GPU is idle most of the time, waiting for requests.

This waste compounds at scale. In a cluster with 100 GPUs, if average utilization is 20%, you’re effectively wasting 80 GPUs worth of compute.

item.title: Deploying vLLM in Production: Lessons Learned
item.description:
Why vLLM?

When we needed to serve large language models at scale, vLLM’s PagedAttention mechanism immediately stood out. Traditional attention implementations allocate the full KV cache upfront, leading to significant memory fragmentation. PagedAttention manages KV cache in fixed-size pages — like virtual memory for LLMs.

The result: up to 24x higher throughput compared to naive implementations.

Production Configuration

Here’s a battle-tested vLLM configuration for production:

from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

llm = LLM(
 model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct",
 tensor_parallel_size=4, # Spread across 4 GPUs
 gpu_memory_utilization=0.90, # Use 90% of VRAM
 max_model_len=32768, # Context window
 max_num_seqs=256, # Concurrent sequences
 enable_chunked_prefill=True, # Better latency/throughput tradeoff
 quantization="awq", # 4-bit quantization
)

Kubernetes Deployment

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
 name: vllm-server
spec:
 replicas: 2
 template:
 spec:
 containers:
 - name: vllm
 image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.6.0
 args:
 - "--model"
 - "Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct"
 - "--tensor-parallel-size"
 - "4"
 - "--gpu-memory-utilization"
 - "0.9"
 resources:
 limits:
 nvidia.com/gpu: "4"
 memory: "128Gi"
 env:
 - name: HUGGING_FACE_HUB_TOKEN
 valueFrom:
 secretKeyRef:
 name: hf-token
 key: token

Common Pitfalls

1. OOM During Peak Load

The fix: set gpu_memory_utilization lower than you think (0.85 vs 0.90) and monitor KV cache hit rates.

item.title: MCP: The USB Standard for AI Context
item.description:
The Context Integration Problem

Every AI application developer faces the same challenge: connecting language models to external data sources, tools, and systems. Before MCP, every integration was custom:

  • OpenAI function calling with custom schemas
  • LangChain tool definitions
  • Proprietary API formats per model provider

The result was a fragmented ecosystem where every AI application had to reimplement the same integrations.
